stories.headline: Republicans Split Over Why They Lost Congress as Vance Blames Iran War
stories.dek: Democrats flipped the House and Senate, and Trump agreed the war hurt the GOP but said he would do it again.
pole_a_bullets: Iran cannot be allowed a nuclear weapon, so the war was necessary even at a political cost.
Vance says the loss came from Trump 2024 voters defecting over the war and costs, not from low turnout.
Vance's fix: end the war, address cost of living, recommit to America First and rethink the Israel relationship.
Some Republicans say the result reflects voter frustration with Congress's productivity. Others say the party must now choose its direction.
pole_b_bullets: The results are a rebuke of Trump, whose endorsed candidates lost across the country.
Jeffries says voters want transformational change and affordability, and vows to focus on both.
Democrats say they will use congressional power to pressure the White House to end the Iran war.
Senate Democrats have sent document-preservation letters ahead of expected investigations of the administration.
stories.pole_a_who: Positions voiced by Trump, Vance, DeSantis and other Republican figures.
stories.pole_b_who: Positions voiced by Hakeem Jeffries, Sen. Mark Kelly and other congressional Democrats.
evidence_left: Democrats won both chambers on Nov. 3, per AP calls. Republicans had held the Senate 53-45 plus two independents caucusing with Democrats (IE University summary of AP calls).
CNN projected Democrats above 250 House seats and at least 30 ousted Republican incumbents as of Nov. 5.
evidence_right: Vance posted on Nov. 4 that the reason Republicans lost was the war. Trump called the comment largely true, per ABC News.
Trump said the war was worth it and that he would do it again, per ABC News and The Washington Post.
stories.sources_line: Sourced from ABC News, CNN, The Washington Post, CBS News, November 08, 2026.

stories.headline: Hot October Jobs Report Revives December Fed Rate-Hike Bets
stories.dek: Payrolls rose 165,000 against much lower forecasts, as traders weigh the Fed's inflation fight against a tech selloff.
pole_a_bullets: The report shows a labor market with momentum, and Fitch's Olu Sonola points to solid GDP and consumer spending too.
Three-month average job growth of 137,000 is far above the prior 12-month pace, which points to a strong underlying economy.
Strong hiring gives the Fed room to focus on inflation without worrying about weak employment, so recession fears recede.
Stocks and Treasuries reacted only mildly, and the S&P 500 and Nasdaq rebounded after Thursday's selloff.
pole_b_bullets: A strong labor market makes rate cuts unlikely, and a further hike is now the base case.
Higher rates cut the present value of future earnings, which hits tech-heavy indexes already in correction.
Inflation has run above target for over five years, and September CPI rose to 3.7%.
Economists warn that high rates could do more damage to housing, consumers and the weaker side of a K-shaped economy.
stories.pole_a_who: Positions commonly voiced by economists and analysts such as Fitch's Olu Sonola.
stories.pole_b_who: Positions commonly voiced by rate-focused strategists and analysts of the AI-stock repricing.
evidence_left: BLS data show 165,000 jobs added in October, with unemployment at 4.1% and wages up 0.4%. August and September were revised up by 84,000 combined (Schwab, Yahoo Finance).
Forecasts differ by outlet: Schwab cited consensus of 65,000, Yahoo Finance 70,000, and Innovative Asset Advisors 59,000.
evidence_right: Reuters reported about 78% market odds of a quarter-point hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting. Schwab cited about 73% from CME FedWatch.
Annual CPI rose from 3.4% to 3.7% in September (The Hill). October CPI is due Nov. 10, per 24/7 Wall St.
stories.sources_line: Sourced from Reuters via Yahoo Finance, Charles Schwab, The Hill, November 08, 2026.

stories.headline: AI Stocks Plunge as Democrats' Win Raises Odds of Tougher AI Rules
stories.dek: The Nasdaq fell into correction Thursday amid fears of a slower AI buildout, then partly rebounded Friday.
pole_a_bullets: Investors read the election as making the AI buildout slower and more expensive, which reprices growth across the supply chain.
The Trump administration has argued against AI-specific regulation and for deregulation to favor industry growth.
Truist's Keith Lerner called the selloff more of a knee-jerk reaction than a real signal about tech under Democratic control.
Congress has not agreed on a bipartisan AI bill, and rushed federal mandates could slow a capital-intensive buildout.
pole_b_bullets: Sen. Maria Cantwell's framework calls for enforceable federal safety standards and continuous testing of frontier AI models.
Her framework also calls for audits of AI developers and protections for children and workers.
Bill Gates has said self-regulation is not enough and that governments should be involved in monitoring.
Democrats say data-center effects on electricity costs and water use were a campaign issue. Newly elected officials have promised conditions on construction.
stories.pole_a_who: Positions commonly voiced by the Trump administration, Wall Street analysts and AI-industry investors.
stories.pole_b_who: Positions commonly voiced by Sen. Maria Cantwell, congressional Democrats and AI-safety advocates.
evidence_left: The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.52% on Nov. 5 and closed in correction. The S&P 500 fell 4.4% and the Dow fell 1,833 points (CNN, AP, CNBC).
Reports differ on the cause: CNN, CNBC and Fox Business cite fears of slower AI buildout after the midterms. NBC News says Qualcomm and Arm earnings triggered it.
evidence_right: Cantwell released a six-point AI framework on Oct. 7 with no legislative text, per Roll Call. She is expected to retake the Senate Commerce chair (PCWorld).
Some lawmakers want Democrats to pass AI safety and data-center bills in January, but the legislative path is unclear (WJLA).
stories.sources_line: Sourced from CNN, NBC News, Roll Call, WJLA, November 08, 2026.
